newsitem.title: CANADA: Suncor examining U.S. refining ventures.
newsitem.headline: Suncor examining U.S. refining ventures.

text.p: Suncor Inc is examining a number of possible deals, including refining joint ventures and purchases, aimed at lessening the blow of widening price spreads between light and heavy oil in the U.S. Midwest, Suncor chief executive Rick George said on Monday.

"It can be anything from a voint venture to purchase to processing arrangement," George told reporters following a ceremony for employees to unveil the Suncor's new name -- Suncor Energy -- and revamped corporate logo.
"It can cover the whole gamut here, we're not only pursuing one avenue, there are a number of avenues we're looking at."
George said widening heavy oil differentials were casting a pall on the future of Suncor's Burnt Lake enhanced heavy oil recovery project in Northern Alberta.

The spread between Canadian Lloydminster heavy and benchmark West Texas Intermediate light oil has recently widened to as much as US$6 per barrel amid growing Canadian supply and head-to-head price competition in the key Midwest market with Venezuelan and Mexican volumes.

"We are looking at whether there are any opportunities downstream of our upstream businesses -- both conventional and the oil sands plant -- that we can look at investments in that chain between those production facilities and the customer," George said.

Suncor is currently developing the Burnt Lake project as a C$15 million steam assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) test. If it gets the go-ahead within an estimated nine to 12 months, it could pump between 40,000 and 50,000 barrels per day of heavy crude.
The pilot plant must be on stream for a number of months before the company can make an assessment of the ultimate production would be, he said.

"The only other part of that equation is that we're very concerned about light-heavy differentials...there's a price at which we would not invest if we cannot get a return on capital above our cost of capital," George said.

He said the company, which plans to spend C$2.0 billion on numerous upstream and downstream projects over four years, was on track to meet its goal of expanding the oil sands operation's production to 105,000 barrels per day by 1999.

The mine, extraction plant and upgrader, located north of Fort McMurray in northeast Alberta, are slated to pump out 85,000 barrels a day of synthetic crude when a major turnaround is completed this spring.

The upgrader expansion, estimated to cost C$300 million, is expected to be finished in about a year and the new Steepbank mine, which also carries a pricetag of C$300 million, is slated to begin producing in late 1998.

Meanwhile, Suncor is examining new exploration projects in Argentina, Brazil and Peru and may be able to announce one in about 12 months, George said, stressing the company is not in the market for acquisitions in the region.

"We're close to fairly high commodity prices, you've got a lot of people looking at acquisitions and my feeling is that whenever yoyu see this industry head in one direction you should probably look in a different direction," he said.
"I'm not saying we would never do acquisitions in these areas but it certainly isn't where we'll be heading in the near term."
